checks.label: So v(t), the sum of the y projections of the component phasors, is just the y projection of the sum of the component phasors: on the first screen, at every length, start angle and moment, the sum arrow's tip is drawn at A's height plus B's height, the two stacked bars end level with the sum's pen, and every drawn point of the sum wave is A's wave plus B's wave

One good use of phasors is for the summing of sinusoids of the same frequency: turning at one speed, the sum arrow keeps one length at every moment, √(floor² + wall²) of the shadows added, and its wave is one sine wave of that length and the same frequency, started at the sum's angle

To determine the vertical component of force the sine function can be used, and the horizontal component the cosine: with the shadows switch on, at every length and start angle of B and every moment, each arrow's floor shadow is drawn its length × cos of its angle and its wall shadow its length × sin, B's starting at A's tip; at the start B's are 6 cos 60° = 3 and 6 sin 60° = 5.196, and the rows add them to 13 and 5.196

The square of any side of a triangle is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides minus twice the product of the other two sides and the cosine of the included angle: at every pair of start angles the drawn sum arrow's length squared is 10² + 6² − 2 × 10 × 6 × cos of the angle inside the tip-to-tail triangle, 180° minus the angle between the arrows, and at the start the rows give 120° and 196 = 14²

Taking a wave away is adding its arrow turned half a turn: B turned to 240° has every height with its sign changed, and A − B is drawn 8.72 long at −36.6°, from floor 10 − 3 = 7 and wall 0 − 5.196 = −5.196; switched off, the sum is 14 long

3-phase systems consist of 3 equal in magnitude voltages and 120 degrees out of phase relative to each other: on the card, at rms and at peak, the three phase arrows are drawn the same length and a third of a turn, 120°, apart

The voltage declared in respect of a low voltage supply shall be 230 volts between the phase and neutral conductors: the card draws each phase arrow 230 V long, its label says so, and its rows start from 230

The square root three is a magnitude multiplier that accompanies a 30 degree phase shift between line voltages and their respective phase voltages: L1 plus L2 turned half a turn is drawn √3 times a phase arrow long, 30° ahead of L1, and the rows give 2 × 230 × sin 60° = 230 × √3 = 398.4 V
The majority of ships have a 3 phase, 3 wire, 440V insulated neutral system: the ship puzzle works from 440 V between lines, and its answer is 440 ÷ √3 = 254 V a phase
Low voltage is a term used to describe 400 V three-phase and 230 V single-phase supplies: the card's line voltage, 230 × √3 = 398.4 V, is read as about 400 V

Phasor diagrams in RMS have the same shape as those drawn using amplitudes, but everything is scaled by a factor of 0.71 = 1/√2: switched to peak, every arrow of the card is drawn √2 times longer in the same direction, a phase reads 325.3 V and the line 563.4 V, and 1 ÷ √2 = 0.71

Sinusoids of different frequencies cannot be represented on the same phasor diagram due to the different speed of the vectors: with B turning twice as fast, the angle between the arrows keeps changing and the drawn sum arrow runs from 1 to 7 long over one turn of A; switched back, it stays 5 long

Every worked number matches the lesson: 5 at 53.1° with slips 7 and 1; 6 cos 60° = 3, 6 sin 60° = 5.196, 13 and 14 at 21.8°; 4 + 2 = 6, 3.464, √48 = 6.93 with slips 8 and 4; 30° with slips 60° and 0.577; 120° and 196; 7, −5.196 and 8.72 at −36.6°; 115, 345, 199.2 and 398.4 V at 30°, 325.3 V and 563.4 V; 398 V with slips 460 V and 230 V; 1 to 7; 254 V with slips 220 V and 762 V; 0 with slips 16 and 11.3; 13 A at 22.6° with slip 17 A; √3 = 1.732, 1 ÷ √2 = 0.71, 4 × √3 = 6.93
